title: Between the Pieces
subtitle: On the covenant God signed alone
teaser: Abram cut the animals, arranged them in two facing rows, and drove the vultures off all afternoon. Then the sun went down, a deep sleep fell on him, and something passed down the corridor he had prepared — without him.
theme: The covenant a person keeps breaking was never being held up by that person.
framework: Jeremiah 31:31-34 — I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts

modules.passage: In the same way, after supper He took the cup, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you.
emphasis: This cup is the new covenant in My blood
modules.scriptureContext: Two minutes with the sentence that takes a six-hundred-year-old promise off the page and puts it in someone's hands.
redLetter: This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you.

modules.definition: covenant — and, in ordinary Greek usage, a will or testament
modules.usage: Most of the Greek Old Testament renders the Hebrew berith with diathēkē — the word for a will, a disposition made by one party on that party's own authority, which the beneficiaries receive rather than negotiate — rather than synthēkē, the word for a negotiated agreement between equals. Whether the translators intended the contrast is debated. The effect is not: the New Testament inherited the word, and it was already in the language centuries before this table.

modules.heading: The Word They Did Not Choose
modules.content:
A treaty and a will are both binding documents, and they work in opposite directions.

A treaty is agreed. Two parties sit down, each brings leverage, terms are negotiated, and the strength of the result depends on both signatures continuing to mean something. If one party defaults, the treaty is in trouble.

A will is not agreed. One person decides, one person disposes, and the beneficiaries are not consulted — their role is to receive. The document's force does not rest on their reliability at all. It rests on the one who made it.

The Greek Old Testament chose the second word, and the New Testament kept it. Which means every time the word covenant appears in these pages, it is arriving with that grammar attached: something one party established and the other party inherits.

And on the last night, Jesus picks up a cup and puts a six-hundred-year-old promise into a present tense. Jeremiah had said the days are coming. Here the days have arrived, and the new arrangement is identified with something being poured out.

The rest of today goes backwards from this table — to the prophet who promised it in the ruins of a nation, and then further back still, to a night in the desert when the whole shape of it was acted out in front of a man who slept through the important part.

modules.prompt: A treaty depends on both signatures continuing to mean something; a will does not. Which of those two has a person been assuming their standing with God is?

modules.heading: A Two-Minute Prayer
modules.prayerText: Lord Jesus, You called it a new covenant and then poured it out, and we have spent years treating it like a contract we might default on. Teach us to receive what we cannot negotiate. Amen.

modules.ctaSubtext: That can be the whole of today. Below, when there is time: a promise made to people whose country was ending, a Hebrew idiom that says covenants are cut rather than signed, a night in the desert where only one party walked the corridor — and a blind Scottish minister who wrote four stanzas in five minutes and never told anyone what had happened to him.

modules.passage: Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah. It will not be like the covenant I made with their fathers when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt— a covenant they broke, though I was a husband to them,” declares the LORD. “But this is the covenant I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the LORD. I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they will be My people. No longer will each man teach his neighbor or his brother, saying, ‘Know the LORD,’ because they will all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest, declares the LORD. For I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more.”
emphasis: a covenant they broke, though I was a husband to them
I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts
modules.scriptureContext: Spoken into the collapse of Judah, to people who had comprehensively failed the previous arrangement, and who are here told the next one will not depend on them keeping it.

modules.heading: A Promise Made to People Who Had Already Failed
modules.content:
The setting matters more than the date. Scholars have argued for a long time about exactly when this oracle was composed — some place it with the prophet himself in the last years before Jerusalem fell, others assign it to a later editorial layer — and the argument is not settled. What is not in dispute is the world it addresses: the collapse of Judah, the end of a kingdom, and a covenant people who had run out of ways to describe their situation as a temporary setback.

Into that, God announces a new arrangement. And the announcement has one striking feature that is easy to read past.

He does not say the old covenant failed. He says they broke it. The blame is not distributed; it is assigned, in the same sentence that promises the replacement. And then a clause that is doing more emotional work than its length suggests: though I was a husband to them.

That clause is where an honest textual note belongs, because the New Testament quotes this passage at length and renders it differently. Hebrews 8, which reproduces Jeremiah 31 nearly whole — at 135 words it is the longest continuous Old Testament quotation anywhere in the New — has "because they did not abide by My covenant, and I disregarded them." Hebrew has a husband; Greek has a turning-away. The New Testament writer is following the Greek Old Testament, which reads differently from the Hebrew at exactly this point. Both readings are ancient. Neither is a mistake. And the difference is worth knowing rather than smoothing over, because a reader with two translations open will find it and deserves to be told why.

What both versions agree on is the structure of the new covenant, and it is stated in a run of first-person verbs. I will make. I will put. I will inscribe. I will be their God. I will forgive. I will remember no more.

There is no corresponding list of obligations. The people in the passage are not assigned a single task.

modules.definition: to cut a covenant — the standard Hebrew idiom for making one
modules.usage: Hebrew does not say a covenant is made, or struck, or entered into. It says a covenant is cut. The verb karath is the ordinary word for cutting — cutting down a tree, cutting off a garment — and it appears about 289 times in the Old Testament. Paired with berith, covenant, it is simply how the language says that an agreement has been established.
modules.usageNote: Which means the idiom carries a memory of how such agreements were originally ratified: something was killed and divided. Genesis 15:18 uses exactly this phrase at the end of a scene in which animals have been halved and laid opposite each other. Every English Bible smooths it to made a covenant; the Hebrew says cut one. The language never lost the picture. Every time an Israelite said the words for making a covenant, he was saying that something had been cut in two.

modules.passage: As the sun was setting, Abram fell into a deep sleep, and suddenly great terror and darkness overwhelmed him. … When the sun had set and darkness had fallen, behold, a smoking firepot and a flaming torch appeared and passed between the halves of the carcasses.
emphasis: a smoking firepot and a flaming torch appeared and passed between the halves
modules.scriptureContext: The scene the idiom remembers. Abram had done the work — brought the animals, split them, arranged the halves opposite each other, and driven the birds of prey off the carcasses all afternoon.

modules.inlineImageAlt: Two facing rows of severed animal halves laid on bare ground forming a straight open corridor, a single small golden flame in the middle of the corridor, and a lone figure lying asleep at the near edge
modules.inlineImageCaption: The corridor Abram prepared, the sleep that took him before it was used, and the one light that moved down it.

modules.heading: What the Text Says, and What It Declines to Say
modules.content:
This scene is preached constantly, and the standard version of it goes further than the evidence does. It is worth getting right, because the accurate version is stronger.

The standard version runs like this: in the ancient world, parties to a covenant walked between severed animals to invoke a curse on themselves — let me be cut in pieces if I break faith — and in Genesis 15 God walks the path alone, taking the self-curse on Himself.

The difficulty is that the two halves of that claim do not appear together outside the Bible. Documents from Mari attest animals killed to ratify a treaty, with no walking between and no curse. Treaty texts from Sefire and an Assyrian treaty of Ashurnirari V contain explicit curses over a cut animal, invoking that fate on whoever breaks faith, with no passing between the pieces. And the one clearly attested rite in which people do walk between severed halves is a Hittite ceremony for the ritual cleansing of a defeated army: a purification, not a covenant, and not a curse.

So the elements the sermon fuses are attested separately and never together — except in the Bible. Jeremiah 34 is the exception, and it is decisive: God describes officials who "passed between the pieces of the calf" and announces that He will treat them like that calf. There, the two halves do join, and the covenanters under the curse are human.

Which throws Genesis 15 into relief. Because Genesis 15 contains no curse language at all.

That silence is not a gap to be filled in from Mari. It is the most unusual thing in the chapter. Every attested rite of this kind puts the *inferior* party under the curse and says the curse out loud. Here the party who could have dictated terms is the one who moves down the corridor, and Scripture does not explain why, and does not attach a formula to it. One scholar states the objection bluntly: we know of no covenant in which the obviously superior party, much less a deity, is put under a potential curse. Even the commentator most often cited for identifying the fire as God's own presence declines the curse reading, calling the rite a dramatic representation of the promises instead.

The honest sentence is therefore narrower than the sermon and heavier than it. The text says a smoking firepot and a flaming torch passed between the halves. It does not name the walker, and the identification of that fire with God's own presence is near-universal. It does not say a curse was invoked. And Abram, who had done every part of the preparation himself, was not on his feet for the part that mattered.

He cut the animals. He arranged them. He spent the afternoon driving vultures off the carcasses — the text is careful to record that he was working. And then the sun went down, and a deep sleep fell on him, and the covenant was ratified by one party in a corridor the other party had built and could not walk.

modules.videoTitle: A Way God Wants to Connect With You (You Might Not Think Much About)
modules.videoCaption: Six minutes on what a covenant actually is in the Bible, how the formal covenants run from Abraham forward, and who finally keeps them.

modules.heading: Two Kinds of Security
modules.ancientTruth: The old covenant was bilateral in its administration: blessings and curses attached to obedience, and the Deuteronomic literature is unembarrassed about it. When Israel broke it, the consequences were exactly what had been specified.
modules.modernApplication: Most people carry a version of the same arrangement internally — an assumption that standing with God rises and falls with the last few weeks of performance, and that the account can be overdrawn.
modules.connectionPoint: Jeremiah's announcement does not soften the terms. It relocates the keeping. The law is not lowered; it is moved — from tablets that can be broken to hearts that God Himself inscribes.
modules.newTestamentEcho: Which is why Hebrews reaches for this passage rather than any other, quoting it at greater length than any other Old Testament text in the New: the writer's whole argument is that the arrangement has changed hands.

modules.heading: Who Supplies the Walking
modules.content:
Monday opened this week with a word: derek, a road as it is actually travelled. The charge against Israel was that they had trusted their own — chosen a route and walked it, and were now standing in the harvest of it.

Ezekiel answers that charge with a sentence that has to be read carefully, because the English translations reach for a word the Hebrew does not use.

"And I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes."

The Hebrew does not contain a causative verb. What it contains is a construction — literally, "and I will do that which — in my statutes you shall walk." Both verbs are ordinary. The force is in the relation between them: God performs the action, and their walking is what that action produces. Not a hand pushing legs, and not a metaphor to be waved at. A stated sequence, with God at the start of it.

Which is the same shape as everything else in this week's second half. Jeremiah's new covenant is a run of first-person verbs with no corresponding list of duties. Genesis 15 is a corridor walked by one party. Hosea asks for a loyalty He had already betrothed Himself to supply.

And all of it converges on a table, on the last night, when a man picks up a cup and says the covenant is in His blood.

Calvin, lecturing on Jeremiah 31, refused the obvious inference that a new covenant meant God had changed His mind. The new covenant is not called new because it contradicts the first, he argued, and it is not a revision issued after the first one disappointed Him. It is the same God, doing the same thing He has been doing since a fire moved down a corridor in the dark, arriving at the point where He does it in person and at His own cost.

Spurgeon, preaching on the verse this whole week is named for, put the mechanism in one line: "He cannot deny his Word, since that Word is Himself, and he cannot deny himself."

Which is why the covenant holds. Not because the terms are lenient. Because the guarantor and the guarantee turn out to be the same person, and He walked the corridor while the other party slept.

modules.heading: Five Minutes in Innellan
modules.content:
His mother found it when he was eighteen months old: the boy's sight was impaired, and the cause was an inflammation behind the eyes that the leading oculist in Glasgow could do nothing about. He kept some vision through school, and by his eighteenth year, for practical purposes, it was gone. It was never quite total — his biographer is careful about that. He had his moments of vision.

Two of his sisters set themselves to learn Latin, Greek and Hebrew so they could read them aloud to him. One of his sisters wrote out his college essays in her own hand, and later took his sermons down from dictation. He was ordained to Innellan, on the Firth of Clyde, in 1868, and preached there while going blind.

On the evening of 6 June 1882 George Matheson was alone in the manse. It was his sister's wedding day and the rest of the family were staying overnight in Glasgow.

And something happened to him.

He never said what. Years later, when he set the circumstances down in writing, this is as far as he went: "Something had happened to me, which was known only to myself, and which caused me the most severe mental suffering. The hymn was the fruit of that suffering."

Then: "It was the quickest bit of work I ever did in my life. I had the impression rather of having it dictated to me by some inward voice than of working it out myself. I am quite sure that the whole work was completed in five minutes, and equally sure that it never received at my hands any retouching or correction."

Four stanzas. The first line was: O Love that wilt not let me go.
modules.connectionToTheme: A great deal has been invented to fill Matheson's silence — most commonly a fiancée who abandoned him over his blindness, a story that appears nowhere in the authorised biography written while his sisters were still alive, and nowhere in any source from his own lifetime. It is not true, and the substitute explanations offered by well-meaning correctors are not documented either. He declined to say, and the declining is the point for this day. The hymn's claim does not rest on anyone knowing what the wound was. A man who could not see, on a night he never described, wrote four stanzas about a love that would not let go — and the authority of that line comes from the same place as the covenant in Genesis 15: from the side that does the holding, not the side being held.

modules.heading: Never Inconsistent With Himself
modules.content: Calvin, refusing the obvious inference that a new covenant meant God had changed His mind: "God is never inconsistent with himself, nor is he unlike himself."
modules.historicalContext: Commentary on Jeremiah, Lecture 123, in John Owen's translation for the Calvin Translation Society. Wednesday's doctrine, landing on Friday's text.

modules.heading: What This Does Not Make Optional
modules.content:
A week that ends here can be misheard, and the misreading is old enough to have a name. If the covenant is kept from God's side, and the walking is supplied, and the law is inscribed rather than posted, then what exactly is left for a person to do?

Jeremiah's own answer is embedded in the promise. "They will all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest." Knowing, in Hosea's vocabulary and in Jeremiah's, is not information. It is the word for what a husband and wife have. The new covenant does not remove the relationship; it is the relationship, finally functioning.

And Ezekiel's construction says the same thing from the other side. God performs the action; their walking is what it produces. The walking still happens. Feet still move. Nothing in the grammar suggests a person is carried.

What has changed is where the reliability lives.

This is the difference between earning the ground under one’s feet and walking on a road somebody else guaranteed. From outside, the two can look identical — both involve getting up, both involve obedience, both involve failure and return. From inside they are nothing alike, because one is load-bearing and the other is not.

And for the reader who arrived at this week exhausted, that distinction is the whole point of five days. Their inconsistency did not dissolve the arrangement, because the arrangement was never resting on it. Their consistency would not have secured it either.

For the reader who arrived managing, the same sentence lands as a demotion. The competence that has been holding everything up was never actually holding it up. It was walking a road that had already been guaranteed, and mistaking the walking for the guarantee.

modules.passage: A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh. And I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and ye shall keep my judgments, and do them.
emphasis: cause you to walk in my statutes
modules.scriptureContext: The same promise as Jeremiah's, in a different prophet's vocabulary — and four verses earlier Ezekiel gives God's reason, which is the reason from Wednesday: "It is not for your sake that I will act… but for My holy name."

modules.prompt: Abram prepared the corridor and slept through its use. Where has a person been trying to walk a path that was never theirs to walk?
additionalQuestions: If standing with God is a will rather than a treaty, what specific anxiety becomes unnecessary this week?
Matheson refused to say what happened to him that night. What would it change to hold a wound without requiring an explanation for it?
The walking still happens; only the guaranteeing has moved. What does that mean for the very next hard thing on the calendar?

modules.heading: A Practice for Today
modules.instruction: An art response — no skill required, and nothing needs to be kept. Ten minutes, paper, one pen.

steps.title: Draw the corridor
steps.description: Two rough rows of shapes down the page, facing each other, with a clear empty lane between them. It does not need to look like anything.

steps.title: Mark the sleeper
steps.description: Put a small mark at the edge of the page, outside the lane, for Abram. Then write beside it the thing currently being carried that has been exhausting to carry.

steps.title: Draw one light
steps.description: Draw a single small flame in the middle of the corridor. One. Then sit with the page for two minutes without adding anything else to it.

modules.heading: The Cup on the Table
modules.content:
The week began with a field and a road and a nation that still had a country. It ends in an upper room with a cup.

What holds the days between them together is a single refusal. At no point does Scripture offer the arrangement most people are quietly running, in which God's commitment tracks human reliability and adjusts accordingly. It never appears. Not in the corridor, not in the prophets, not at the table.

What appears instead is a God who will not go back on Himself, and who has arranged matters so that the covenant's survival depends on that fact rather than on anybody's grip.

Genesis declines to explain why He walked the corridor alone. It simply records that He did, and that the man who had spent the day preparing it was unconscious when it happened. Two thousand years later, give or take, a man holds up a cup on the night before He is arrested and says the new covenant is in His blood — and the corridor finally gets its explanation, in person, at His own cost.

Tomorrow this reading gathers the week into one page. Sunday it stops talking. But the sentence to carry out of today is the one Matheson wrote in five minutes on a night he never described, having lost the sight he was never going to get back: O Love that wilt not let me go.

He did not write: O Love that I have managed to hold on to.

modules.heading: Closing Prayer
modules.prayerText: Father, we have been treating this as a treaty and grading our own compliance, and we are tired. You cut the covenant while Abram slept. You promised a law written inside rather than posted outside. You said You would act, and that our walking would be what Your acting produced. We have nothing to add to that and nothing to secure it with. Take the anxiety we have called responsibility. Put Your Spirit in us and let the walking follow. And when we wake in the night rehearsing our own reliability, remind us whose blood is in the cup. Amen.
modules.breathPrayer: Breathing in: You walked the corridor. Breathing out: I was asleep, and it held.

modules.heading: Today's Commitment
modules.commitment: I will stop auditing my standing with God as though it were a contract I might default on, and I will receive it as something already disposed in my favour.
leavingAtCross: The ledger where I have been scoring my own compliance
The assumption that my grip is what keeps this from failing
The exhaustion of walking a corridor I was never asked to walk
receivingFromCross: A covenant cut and ratified from one side
A law written inside rather than posted outside
A cup poured out before anyone had improved

modules.heading: One Question
modules.question: What is genuinely unusual about the covenant ceremony in Genesis 15?
options: Animals were killed, which was rare in ancient covenant-making
The superior party is the one who passes between the pieces — and the text attaches no curse formula at all, which matches nothing in the surrounding cultures
It is the only covenant in the Bible with no promises attached
Abram negotiated the terms before agreeing
modules.explanation: Animal slaughter at treaty-making is well attested, and so are curses invoked over a cut animal — but in the surrounding evidence those elements appear separately, and the curse always falls on the lesser party. Genesis 15 has the greater party move down the corridor and says nothing about a curse, and Abram is asleep. The silence is the striking feature, not a gap to be filled in.

modules.heading: The Voice Behind Today
modules.name: George Matheson
modules.bio: A Scottish minister who lost most of his sight in childhood and preached for nearly forty years — at Innellan on the Firth of Clyde from 1868, then at St Bernard's in Edinburgh from 1886. He was a serious scholar as well as a preacher, and his sisters learned biblical languages in order to read to him.
modules.keyQuote: I am quite sure that the whole work was completed in five minutes, and equally sure that it never received at my hands any retouching or correction.
modules.lessonForUs: Matheson is here for what he did not say. He named the suffering and withheld its cause for the rest of his life, and the hymn has outlived him by well over a century without anyone knowing. Some things hold without an explanation attached, which is the same claim Genesis 15 makes about a corridor in the dark.

modules.heading: Sources & Further Study

relatedScriptures.text: Where the covenant rite's teeth are visible: officials who "passed between the pieces of the calf," and God announcing He will treat them like that calf. The one place passing-between and self-curse clearly join — and there the covenanters are human.
Jeremiah 31 quoted nearly whole, following the Greek Old Testament — at 135 words, the longest continuous Old Testament quotation in the New Testament.
The whole scene: the stars, the believing that was credited as righteousness, Abram driving the birds of prey away, and the covenant cut at the end of it.
God's stated reason, four verses before the new heart: "It is not for your sake that I will act… but for My holy name" — Wednesday's argument, arriving in Friday's passage.

resources.title: D. Macmillan, The Life of George Matheson (Hodder & Stoughton, 1907), pp. 181-182
resources.description: Source of Matheson's own account of 6 June 1882, quoted verbatim, and of the details of his blindness and his sisters. The widely told story that a fiancée abandoned him over his failing sight appears nowhere in this authorised biography — written with family cooperation while his sisters were living — nor in any source from his lifetime, and is not used here. "O Love That Wilt Not Let Me Go" was first published in Life and Work, January 1883.

resources.description: Quoted verbatim from John Owen's translation for the Calvin Translation Society (Edinburgh, 1850-55), free at ccel.org.

resources.title: C. H. Spurgeon, sermon no. 1453, Metropolitan Tabernacle Pulpit vol. 25 (1879)
resources.description: Spurgeon's sermon on 2 Timothy 2:13, the source of the line on the Word and the Speaker being the same. The SpurgeonGems edition modernises spelling and capitalises deity pronouns; the 1879 setting does not.

resources.title: On the ancient Near Eastern background
resources.description: The comparative evidence is genuinely mixed and this reading has tried to represent it honestly. Mari attests donkey slaughter as treaty ratification without any passing between the pieces or curse. Sefire and the treaty of Ashurnirari V contain explicit similitude curses over a cut animal, with no passing between. A Middle Hittite ritual (KUB XVII 28 iv 45-56, studied by Olivier Masson in Revue de l'histoire des religions 137/1, 1950) has troops march between halved animals — as a purification of a defeated army, not a covenant. Gerhard Hasel, sympathetic to the comparative approach, concedes that the rite in Genesis 15 still has no exact extrabiblical parallel. David L. Petersen objects that no known covenant places the superior party under a curse; Gordon Wenham, usually cited for identifying the fire as a theophany, reads the rite as a dramatic representation of the promises rather than a dramatised curse. There is also a circularity worth knowing: arguments from second-millennium parallels assume an early date for Genesis 15, and that date is itself contested.

resources.title: Hebrew and Greek data
resources.description: karath (H3772), "to cut," about 289 Old Testament occurrences; berith (H1285), "covenant," 284; the idiom karath berith appears at Genesis 15:18. diathēkē (G1242) is the Septuagint's choice for berith over synthēkē, and carries the sense of a will disposed by one party. On Ezekiel 36:27: the Hebrew is וְעָשִׂ֗יתִי אֵ֣ת אֲשֶׁר־בְּחֻקַּי֙ תֵּלֵ֔כוּ, and both verbs are ordinary Qal forms — the causal force is in the relation between the clauses, not in a causative verb stem, and this reading has been careful not to claim otherwise.

modules.forDeeperStudy: Read Genesis 15 whole, then Jeremiah 31:31-34, then Hebrews 8, then Luke 22:14-20 in one sitting. The question to carry through all four: in each passage, who is holding the covenant up — and what is the other party doing at the time?
